chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn al-Ansari, from Yahya ibn Ma'la al-Aslami, from Hashim ibn Yazid, who said:

I heard Zayd ibn Ali (peace be upon him) saying: Ali (peace be upon him) had greater reward in his war than his standing with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) in his war. I said: With what do you say this, may Allah rectify you? He said to me: Because he was with the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) a follower, and he did not have except the reward of his followership. And in this [war], he was the one being followed, and he had the reward of everyone who followed him.

key_terms.تَابِعاً: A follower (one who follows a leader)
key_terms.زَيْدُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ: Zayd ibn Ali, a prominent Imam from the Ahl al-Bayt

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam Ali receive greater reward in his own war than when fighting with the Prophet?
ai.summary: Zayd ibn Ali highlights the theological principle of 'ajr al-matbu' (reward of the leader) by contrasting Imam Ali’s status as a follower (tabi') during the Prophet’s era with his role as the supreme leader (matbu') in his own campaigns. This distinction underscores the Shia belief that the Imam’s independent authority grants him the cumulative reward of all his followers, a concept central to understanding the spiritual hierarchy in Shia jurisprudence and theology.
